title: Give learners clear, accessible recovery messages
sources: W3C WCAG 2.2 Recommendation: Error Identification, Error Suggestion, and Status Messages
Python 3.14 documentation: gettext and Unicode strings
masterChecklist: Accessibility, reliability, error messages, internationalization, privacy-aware logging
Ethical engineering: accessibility, privacy, data minimization, auditability, user safety, responsible automation
whyItMatters: A vague error leaves a beginner stuck. Clear text naming the field and next action helps users recover and gives a web interface a message it can present to assistive technology.
simpleExplanation: Keep an internal error code separate from a user-facing message. The message should name what went wrong in familiar language and what the learner can do next. In a web page, the interface must associate that text with the relevant field and announce status changes through appropriate semantics; a Python function alone cannot prove the page is accessible.
mentalModel: An error code is the repair-shop ticket number. The visible message is the instruction the customer can follow.
outcomes: Return a stable error code and useful recovery text.
Explain what an actual UI must do beyond generating a Python string.

realWorldExample.scenario: A progress CSV row has a blank minutes value.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: The site shows only a red icon and a Python ValueError traceback, so the learner cannot find or repair the row.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Return a safe code, row number, and plain-language suggestion; the UI places it near the upload control and exposes it as text to assistive technology.

explanation: The internal code remains stable for program logic while the sentence can improve or be translated.
The row number gives a repairable location without copying the private row into the message.
The fallback avoids displaying a raw traceback or an unfamiliar internal code.
The web UI still needs a labelled control and an accessible status presentation; this function only supplies text.
workedExample.expectedOutput: Row 3 has no study minutes. Add a number and try again.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Pass an unknown code and check that the fallback contains a next action but no raw exception details.

procedure: Define one stable internal error code for each repairable condition.
Write a short message naming the affected field or safe row number.
Tell the user what to change or what to try next.
Keep private values, paths, stack traces, and credentials out of the visible message.
For a web UI, associate the message with the relevant control and test keyboard, screen-reader, and narrow-screen presentation.
Keep user-facing sentences together for future translation; avoid assembling grammar from many fragments.

commonMistakes.mistake: Showing only color or an icon for failure.
commonMistakes.why: The status may not be perceived or understood by every user.
commonMistakes.avoid: Provide explicit visible text and appropriate programmatic status.

commonMistakes.mistake: Printing a raw traceback as the only learner message.
commonMistakes.why: It may expose internals and rarely tells the user how to recover.
commonMistakes.avoid: Translate known errors into safe, actionable guidance.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a well-written Python string proves a web page accessible.
commonMistakes.why: Focus order, labels, semantics, and status announcements are separate UI behavior.
commonMistakes.avoid: Test the rendered interaction with keyboard and assistive technology.

lab.title: Write a recoverable CSV error
lab.safety: The lab uses fictional row numbers and no private learner data.
lab.starterCode:
def import_feedback(code, row_number):
    # Return code and message for missing_minutes.
    # Return a safe fallback for unknown codes.
    pass
guidedSteps: For missing_minutes, mention the row and minutes field.
Give a concrete correction and retry action.
For unknown codes, return a generic safe instruction.
Test both cases without putting raw row content into either message.
checks: Known error names the row and repair.
Unknown error offers a safe next step.
Neither message exposes a traceback or private row.
The internal code remains separate from visible text.
hints: Return a dictionary with code and message keys.
Use an f-string for the safe row number.
Keep a complete sentence in each branch.
lab.solutionExplanation: The function returns program-readable reason data alongside a beginner-readable correction. An interface must still render this message accessibly.
challenges: Draft the control label and status announcement for a web upload screen.
Replace the row number with a safe run ID for an unexpected error.

projectConnection.milestone: Add consistent, accessible invalid-input feedback to the CSV importer and capstone UI.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: A learner can identify a bad row and its repair in text; a keyboard and screen-reader review confirms that the rendered page exposes the status.

assessment.question: Why keep an error code separate from the visible message?
assessment.answer: The code supports stable program decisions while the message can be clear and translated.
assessment.explanation: A raw code is not enough guidance for a learner.

assessment.question: What must a web UI do beyond producing a Python error string?
assessment.answer: Associate text with the relevant control and expose status changes through accessible semantics.
assessment.explanation: Accessibility depends on rendered interaction, not just wording.

assessment.question: What should a repairable CSV message include?
assessment.answer: A safe row or field location and a specific next action.
assessment.explanation: This helps the learner correct the input without exposing private data.
